ARBITER results against blinded expert ratings

Two blinded human experts independently rated every trial domain without AI. The figures and tables below use the frozen independent ratings and the separate forced-choice endpoint.

Results

All 102 trials from 16 meta-analyses received two independent expert assessments of all 510 domain cells (Figure 3).

Among cells where the arms disagreed and the adjudicators made the same forced choice, they preferred ARBITER’s rating in 53/60 (88.3%; 95% CI 79.7–96.3; Figure 4).

Adjudicator 1 independently agreed with ARBITER on 371/510 cells (72.7%), Unassisted on 332/510 (65.1%) and Published on 301/510 (59.0%); the paired ARBITER − Unassisted difference was 7.6 percentage points (95% CI 5.1–10.2; Table 1).

Adjudicator 2 independently agreed with ARBITER on 433/510 cells (84.9%), Unassisted on 400/510 (78.4%) and Published on 362/510 (71.0%); the paired ARBITER − Unassisted difference was 6.5 percentage points (95% CI 3.5–9.4; Table 1).

On the 81 trials with observed Published Overall, the paired ARBITER − Unassisted difference in agreement with derived Overall was 13.6 percentage points (95% CI 6.2–21.0) for Adjudicator 1 and 17.3 (8.6–25.9) for Adjudicator 2 (Table 1).

For ARBITER ratings stricter than Published, the independent expert rating matched ARBITER in 64/88 cells for Adjudicator 1 and 65/88 for Adjudicator 2 (Figure 5B).

Unassisted broke the RoB 2 rules in 65/509 evaluable domain ratings (12.8%; 95% CI 10.0–15.6), while all 1407/1407 cited text records were bound to quotations found in content-hashed stored sources (Table 2).

Agreement with Published was poor for both arms (weighted κ 0.34 for ARBITER and 0.28 for Unassisted; Table 3).

Median [IQR] system runtime was 7.6 [6.1–10.5] minutes per trial for ARBITER and 0.5 [0.4–0.5] for Unassisted; API list-price equivalents were US$3.78 [3.46–4.10] and US$0.09 [0.07–0.13] per trial, respectively (eTable 16).

Rules-only recomputation changed 26 Unassisted domain ratings, including 6 of the original arm-discordant cells. On the 60 cells with an agreed forced choice, Unassisted matched that choice in 7 cells before recomputation and 8 afterwards. Agreement with the independent ratings fell from 332/510 to 324/510 for Adjudicator 1 and from 400/510 to 391/510 for Adjudicator 2; applying the rule fix did not raise agreement with either expert (eTable 6).

Across evaluable signalling answers, collapsed agreement was 80.4% and 74.9% for ARBITER and Unassisted against Adjudicator 1, and 90.9% and 87.4% against Adjudicator 2. On paired answers, the ARBITER − Unassisted differences were 5.0 percentage points (95% CI 3.6–6.4) and 3.3 (1.9–4.7), respectively (Figure 6; eTable 5).

For Adjudicator 1, the largest collapsed domain gap was in D5: 11.3 percentage points (95% CI 8.2–14.6). For Adjudicator 2, the D5 gap was 3.7 (95% CI −0.3 to 7.4), and the largest gap was in D3 (7.9; 95% CI 2.8–13.6). Question-specific paired differences are shown in Figure 6 and domain-level agreement in eFigure 2.

Within-direction choices (Y↔︎PY or N↔︎PN) accounted for about half of five-level disagreements against Adjudicator 1 (ARBITER 322/617, 52.2%; Unassisted 377/732, 51.5%) and about three-quarters of five-level disagreements against Adjudicator 2 (ARBITER 368/504, 73.0%; Unassisted 388/566, 68.6%) (eTable 5); cross-direction counts include NI versus either direction.

The experts independently agreed on 388/510 domain ratings (76.1%; weighted κ 0.59); agreement was lowest in D3 (54/102; eTable 8).

Legends and alt text: Figures 1–2

Figure 1. ARBITER splits the work: an AI model reads and answers; rule-based software checks quotes, applies RoB 2 rules and records everything. Lanes show the reviewer, AI model, ARBITER server and audit file across capture, approval, domain assessment and export. Plain labels show actions; grey text names the underlying tool calls. The reviewer receives the HTML report and audit file, both checkable by an independent verifier. RoB 2 is the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomised trials.

Alt text: The reviewer chooses a trial and outcome and approves the result to assess. The AI model reads reports, selects evidence and answers questions. ARBITER stores source records, checks quotes and applies the RoB 2 rules. The reviewer receives an HTML assessment report and an audit file containing sources, quotes, answers and decisions; both can be checked by an independent verifier.

Figure 2. Each answer is tied to stored sources, and RoB 2 rules compute the rating across every domain. AVATAR compares early surgery with watchful waiting in asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis; the outcome is all-cause death. This trial was chosen to illustrate the process, not as representative. Rows link paraphrased questions, source excerpts, AI answers, software checks and domain ratings. Letter/page tabs identify sources; “Weighed against” and “Open point” give counter-evidence and unknowns. A missing dated analysis plan leads to Some concerns overall. Full answers and official question wording appear in the AVATAR complete trace in the supplement. Y, yes; PY, probably yes; PN, probably no; N, no; NI, no information.

Alt text: AVATAR’s five risk-of-bias domains connect source excerpts to the AI model’s answers and the ratings computed by ARBITER. Four domains are Low. For selection of the reported result, the stored sources do not establish a dated plan for this analysis. The model answers No information, and the RoB 2 rules yield Some concerns for that domain and overall. Counter-evidence and unresolved questions remain visible alongside the answers.

Figure 3 Every domain cell received two blinded independent ratings. The nested subsets identify disputed cells, arm-discordant cells and equal forced choices. Side notes identify cells with three concordant labels, which give no forced-choice information, and Overall derived from each expert’s domain ratings. Independent ratings and signalling answers were frozen before labels were shown. The three excluded trials had unsupported designs. Alt text: Included trials lead to two complete expert assessments, followed by nested preference subsets.

Figure 4 Adjudicators preferred ARBITER in most arm disagreements. Rows are grouped as Primary (agreed choice), Sensitivity (each adjudicator; split cells counted as losses), and Post hoc strata. The primary row retains equal forced choices; expert-specific rows retain all arm disagreements. Split decisions count as ARBITER losses without assigning a win to Unassisted. Blue circles show ARBITER, with no marker encoding for adjudicator. Right-hand labels show ARBITER count/denominator and the Unassisted count; ties can credit both arms. The dashed line marks equal preference. Alt text: Grouped forest of primary, sensitivity and strictness estimates of ARBITER preference. CI, confidence interval; 10,000 percentile bootstrap replicates, trials resampled within meta-analysis; seed 20261018.

Figure 5 Independent experts agreed more often with ARBITER. A, Exact agreement against each expert by domain and derived Overall; the dashed line is expert-to-expert agreement. ARBITER is a blue circle, Unassisted an orange square and Published a dark-grey triangle, in that legend and dodge order. Adjudicators are separated by facet. B, Each horizontal bar partitions directional disagreements into expert matches arm (medium grey), matches Published (light grey), or matches neither (near white). Segment labels give count/n; ARBITER rows precede Unassisted rows. When ARBITER was stricter, the experts matched Published in only 5/88 and 14/88 cells, respectively. A, D1–D5: n = 102 per domain and expert; Overall: n = 102 for ARBITER, Unassisted and expert-to-expert agreement, and n = 81 for Published. Twenty-one (21) published reviews gave no Overall label and are excluded. Main Table 1 uses the same n = 81 Overall trials for all three sources. Directional CIs are in eTable 9. Alt text: Domain and Overall agreement against each expert, above three-part directional disagreement bars. CI, confidence interval; 10,000 percentile bootstrap replicates, trials resampled within meta-analysis; seed 20261018.

Figure 6 ARBITER generally agreed more often with the experts on individual signalling questions. Question-level paired ARBITER − Unassisted differences compare collapsed agreement with each expert’s independent answer. Blue circles encode the ARBITER contrast, with expert identity and n printed on each row, grouped by domain. Collapsed agreement combines Y/PY and N/PN, with NI separate. Only explicit matched answers evaluable in both arms contribute. Questions with fewer than 20 paired answers are omitted: 2.4 (Adjudicator 1, n = 0); 2.4 (Adjudicator 2, n = 0); 2.5 (Adjudicator 1, n = 0); 2.5 (Adjudicator 2, n = 0); 2.7 (Adjudicator 1, n = 5); 2.7 (Adjudicator 2, n = 5); 3.4 (Adjudicator 1, n = 19); 4.4 (Adjudicator 1, n = 15); 4.4 (Adjudicator 2, n = 16); 4.5 (Adjudicator 1, n = 5); 4.5 (Adjudicator 2, n = 4). All questions, including these sparse rows and the five-level scale, are shown in eFigure 3 and eTable 5. Domain-level agreement is in eFigure 2. Alt text: Collapsed per-question paired differences and intervals for both experts, grouped by domain. Within-direction choices (Y↔︎PY or N↔︎PN) accounted for about half of five-level disagreements against Adjudicator 1 (ARBITER 322/617, 52.2%; Unassisted 377/732, 51.5%) and about three-quarters of five-level disagreements against Adjudicator 2 (ARBITER 368/504, 73.0%; Unassisted 388/566, 68.6%) (eTable 5); cross-direction counts include NI versus either direction. CI, confidence interval; 10,000 percentile bootstrap replicates, trials resampled within meta-analysis; seed 20261018.

eFigure 1 Published label agreement varied across reviews. ARBITER uses blue circles and Unassisted orange squares, in that legend and dodge order. Marks show weighted κ and its interval. CI, confidence interval; 10,000 percentile bootstrap replicates, trials resampled within meta-analysis; seed 20261018.

eFigure 2 Domain level signalling agreement. ARBITER uses blue circles and Unassisted orange squares; experts and answer scales are separated by facet. All denominators and exact values are in eTable 5. CI, confidence interval; 10,000 percentile bootstrap replicates, trials resampled within meta-analysis; seed 20261018.

eFigure 3 All signalling question paired differences. The Figure 6 display includes all sparse questions here. Blue circles encode ARBITER − Unassisted, with expert and n in each row label. The two columns separate collapsed and five-level answers. CI, confidence interval; 10,000 percentile bootstrap replicates, trials resampled within meta-analysis; seed 20261018.

Each source cell reports exact agreement n/N (%) and linearly weighted κ. Differences are ARBITER − Unassisted exact agreement in percentage points (95% CI). Overall uses the same 81 trials with observed Published Overall for every source; 21 published labels are missing and excluded. Agreed-reference Overall retains 42 of these trials. Mean of experts is the arithmetic mean of the two expert-specific estimates, not pooled independent observations; only percentages and κ are displayed for this row. Its difference is the mean of the two expert-specific paired differences; the CI is the percentile interval of their mean within each shared bootstrap replicate. The agreed reference retains cells with equal independent expert ratings (388 domain cells; 42 matched Overall trials). The expert-to-expert foot row compares the two independent ratings. Full estimates, all-trial Overall (102 trials; agreed reference 52) and all paired contrasts appear in eTable 2. CI, confidence interval; 10,000 percentile bootstrap replicates, trials resampled within meta-analysis; seed 20261018.

Yes, documented; No, affirmative absence; NR, Not reported (presence or absence unclear). Partly means: code, spreadsheet or incomplete rules; enforcement, some configurations or incomplete answer checks; breaks, overall-only or qualitative checks; quotations, semantic judging without occurrence/integrity checks; audit, retained responses without a verifiable source bundle; agent, enabled browsing or retrieval without demonstrated agent tool calls; reference, limited re-review, historical independent teams or text-relevance review; registry/protocol, compressed or restricted delivery. Structured prompting alone is not enforced rules. Registry/protocol includes SAPs and available records; a registration number alone does not qualify. This study gave both compared arms identical inputs; other matched model/workflow comparisons also used identical underlying sources (see eTable 21). a, Compressed ancillary records; overall-only checks. b, Post hoc Excel derivation; six development trials. c, Prompt rules. d, RoB 2 cohort; protocols when available. e, Masked panel; actual browsing unmeasured. f, One trial, 38 runs. g, Retrieval and retained edits. h, Post hoc support judging. i, ROBINS-I; selected concordant references. j, Recorded overrides permitted; none in 510 domains; blinded dual expert rating of all domains. k, RobotReviewer used RoB 1; its blinded panel judged text relevance. Reference callouts resolve in the manuscript bibliography. Condensed cell evidence and quotation locations: eTable 21.

Reproduction

The analysis pipeline, test suite and output verifier reproduce these results. The numerical CSVs and source traces accompany the figures. Supplementary methods and results provide all secondary estimates and reporting details. Trial PDFs are not redistributed.
